lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah say goodbye, and look back
lead.head: The flow stops, the stock stays
body: “For the last time, I’m Amit and this is Ajay.” With that, Amit Varma opened the final episode of *Everything is Everything*, the weekly show he and Ajay Shah have made for two and a half years.
Neither host wanted to stop, Varma said. Each had reasons, and when the two talked, the reasons coincided. “All good things come to an end,” he said. “Better things lie ahead of both of us.”

Shah’s main reason was that he had said what he wanted to say. A lifetime of hiking gives one episode, a lifetime of cycling another, a lifetime of poker another. “One can’t live more lives and create these bodies of knowledge,” he said. {128-S01}

As the show moved away from that lifetime material, the episodes grew harder and costlier to make. Shah is also writing a book on taxes with Vijay Kelkar and Arvind Modi, and has three conferences to run in early December.

Varma’s reason was bandwidth. The show came out every Friday at 12 o’clock, he said, even when he was in hospital and when Shah broke his leg. But he also produced it, and it was on his mind all the time. {128-S02}
He wants to write, and to take a pause. “On our own, we would not have stopped the show,” he said.
## A single picture
Looking back, Shah said he was “truly happy and proud”. He wanted to claim something for the show.
India, he said, is a country where statism is all-pervasive. Attempts to reimagine it have been piecemeal, and a piecemeal reform fails when everything around it is distorted by the state.
The show, he argued, offers a complete picture instead, with people, freedom, consent and agency at the heart of the story. {128-C01}
Taken together, he said, the episodes answer “this biggest of all stories”: why India is poor, and why its capital and labour are not mobilised into high-quality firms. {128-C02}

Varma described it differently. The show, he said, “fused public purpose with private passion”: alongside the state, firms and finance sat reading, chess, cricket, poker and stories that should be films.
## Seven lessons
Shah then asked for the higher-order lessons. Varma, who said the show had shaped him, gave seven, addressed to creators.

Have a bias for action. Don’t let perfection get in the way of production. Be loved by a few rather than liked by many. Be authentic. Build community. Use the freedom that comes from owning the means of production. Play the long game.

Running through them was the economist’s distinction between stock and flow. A book is stock: it outlives its author. A weekly show is flow, to be thought aloud and put out. But over time, Varma said, a body of flow becomes stock.
The episodes, he said, remain out there for everyone to watch. In that sense, the show isn’t over.
## Not quite the end
Shah would not call it an end. “Everything that dies, some day it comes back,” he said, urging Varma to resurrect the show in some form. {128-J07}
Varma does want to do more on YouTube one day, but not under this name. *Everything is Everything*, he said, is the two of them.
“The journey’s been great,” he said. “So thank you Ajay for coming on our journey with me.”
“Thank you, Amit,” Shah replied, “for bringing me to this journey.”

second.label: The co-host question
second.head: No understudy for Ajay
second.deck: Amit Varma on why the show will not carry on with someone else
body: Ajay Shah urged Amit Varma to resurrect the show: the ethos, the people and the audience were all still there. Others suggested Varma carry on with a new co-host. {128-S07}

The first name that came to mind was Pranay Kotasthane, whom both hosts deeply admire. Varma talked to him, and Kotasthane’s view, which Varma shares, was that the show was its two hosts and nobody else.

Varma and Kotasthane may make a separate, fun show one day, with Bollywood and Hindi in it. Under this name, it would feel odd. Varma always meant the channel to carry several shows. For this one, he said, “the journey is done”. {#journeydone}

quote.text: Everything is Everything is you and me. People associate it with us.

second.caption: why there will be no new co-host

third.head: Two years, no peeking
body: When the show began, Amit Varma sat Ajay Shah down and proposed a deal: they would make it for two years without looking at the numbers. “Now this man did not obey me,” Varma said. “He kept looking at the analytics.” {128-S05}
The idea came from Ali Abdaal, who once said that anyone starting a YouTube channel should not look at the numbers for two years. {#abdaal}

Varma’s reasoning was that the moment outside applause matters, you start dumbing yourself down and drift from the authenticity that makes you special. Validation never comes early anyway, he said, “because you will suck at the start”.
Shah came a long way regardless. “When we started, you were so awkward and clumsy,” Varma said. “Today you’re a consummate professional.”
third.caption: the two-year pact

p2.title: This body of work
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why they stopped, what they built, and what it taught them

sections.label: The reasons
sections.head: Said what he had to say
sections.caption: one lifetime of knowledge
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah each had reasons to end the show, and when they talked, they found the reasons coincided. Shah had two: “one big reason” and “a less big reason”.
The big one was that nice, complete episodes come out of lifetimes of knowledge, and there are not many of them. Shah has one lifetime, he said, and he had said what he wanted to say. {128-S01}

The less big one was cost. As the conversation moved away from familiar lifetime material, the work grew harder. He is writing a book on taxes with Vijay Kelkar and Arvind Modi, and runs three conferences in early December. “It is just a gruelling pace,” he said. {#conferences}

Varma had hoped for a different list. “When you said so many, I was hoping you’re gonna say so many books,” he said; he has been urging Shah to write several, among them *Invisible Infrastructure*. {128-J01}
## Bandwidth, not logistics

Varma’s own reason was mental space. Shooting took three days every six weeks. Producing, which he also did, meant building the list of on-screen inserts for each episode and talking over the edit every day. “It was taking up mind space,” he said.
He loves the show and would not have stopped on his own, but he wants to write.
~ Varma would rather end on a note where they can look back with happiness. “No man steps in the same river twice,” he said. {128-J06}

quote.text: I have one lifetime of knowledge. I have only one lifetime of knowledge.

sections.label: The body of work
sections.head: Solow’s model, opened up
sections.caption: the Solow model
body: Ajay Shah wanted to “claim something important”. India, he said, is a country where statism is all-pervasive and “more and more state coercion” is the default answer to everything.

Efforts to reimagine the country have been piecemeal, and no single reform works when everything around it is distorted by the state. The show, Shah argued, offers a complete picture, with people, freedom, consent and agency at its heart. The state is needed, “but it’s not the essence”. {128-C01}
## Three black boxes
Then he went “one step bigger”. The crude Solow model makes output a function of labour, capital and one magic number, productivity. After independence, people read it causally.

Every term, Shah said, hides a deeper story. India’s employment rate is something like 36 or 38 per cent of people aged 16 to 64. {#employment} In China the ratio is double. The problem is not a shortage of people but that firms are not forming to put them to work.

There is infinite capital in the world economy, yet India has not opened its capital account to bring down the cost of capital. Low productivity comes from a thousand institutional failures to create checks and balances and creative destruction. {128-C02}
~ Amit Varma’s gloss was that the show had fused public purpose with private passion, the policy beside reading, chess, cricket and poker. {128-C03}

quote.text: We’ve told this biggest of all stories that why is India poor?

sections.label: The first lessons
sections.head: Done is the road to right
sections.caption: stock and flow
body: The show taught Amit Varma nothing radically new, he said, but hardened ideas he held vaguely. The first: have a bias for action.

He called it “a dangerous phrase”: Ajay Shah has often argued that the state, whose every act is deeply consequential, should move gradually. {128-C04} For creators, though, “bias for action is good, go for it.”

The second lesson came from their friend Vinay Sitapati: “Don’t let perfection get in the way of production.” {128-J09} Every episode has something wrong with it, Varma admitted, and he still cringes at his own footage.
## Stock and flow

A related frame came from economics. Stock is like wealth: it stays. Flow is like income: it keeps coming. For a creator, books are stock, such as *In Service of the Republic* and Shah’s forthcoming book on taxation. Columns, blog posts, newsletters and weekly shows are flow. {128-C06}
Varma took an image from Philip Larkin’s poem *This Be the Verse*, in which misery “deepens like a coastal shelf”. Knowledge is a coastal shelf too, he said, and stock goes into its layers. {128-R17}
~ So agonise over a book, he said, but with flow, think aloud and put it out. Doing so makes you a better thinker, and the feedback finds holes in your argument.

quote.text: In fact, getting it done is the path to getting it right. Production is a path to perfection.

sections.label: Three, four, five
sections.head: Better loved than liked
sections.caption: being loved by a few
body: Amit Varma’s third lesson was a line from Paul Graham, who used it of startups: it is better to be loved by a few than liked by many. {128-R19}

Fewer numbers bring deeper engagement, Varma said. Every time he goes to Blossom’s bookstore in Bangalore, two people come up to him. {#blossoms} The show’s comment section, he reported with pride, is wonderful, and he has met three or four people through their comments.
Chasing whatever is trending, by contrast, is “a path to mediocrity”, because everybody is chasing it. {128-C07}
## Just be yourself
The fourth lesson: “It is both easy and rewarding to be authentic.” Over a long run, Varma said, any pretence produces contrived content that others see through. {128-C08}
Being yourself, he added, is the only thing that sets you apart from “the other eight billion people on this planet”.

The fifth lesson was community, the only thing, Varma said, that a creator can monetise. {128-C09} Readers already pay with their time and attention, even when an article is free: “My time is worth money.” The publisher and the advertiser, the two middlemen of the old model, are going away.
~ Yet the hosts never bothered to monetise their community, he said, “because that’s not the point”.

quote.text: If you are a creator and you want to monetise, you can only monetise the community, the people who really care about you.

sections.label: The last lessons
sections.head: No gatekeeper required
sections.caption: the freedom of form
body: Amit Varma’s sixth lesson was freedom. Take a show like this one to mainstream media, he said, and they would laugh the hosts out of the room: inflation targeting, the bankruptcy code, and two hosts who “aren’t even like glamorous, amazing people”.
*The Seen and the Unseen*, with its ten-hour conversations with economists, would have fared no better. {128-J04}

But creators now have the means of production at hand, Varma said. There is no gatekeeper, and form is free: one hour, 90 minutes, two hours, or one conversation split into two episodes. {128-C10} “Creative”, he added, covers educators and social-sector thinkers as much as writers and filmmakers.
## The long game

The seventh lesson was to play the long game, which Varma called a lesson in public policy too. {#longgame} Forget whether the lighting is good or what your friends will say, he said, and be internally driven.
The moment outside applause matters, he argued, you start dumbing yourself down. And early applause never comes, because everyone is bad at the start. You get better only by constant iteration.
~ In that sense, he said, the show is not over: “these episodes are still out there for you for everyone to watch.”

quote.text: We didn’t have to go through a gatekeeper, we had the means of production at our hands, we didn’t have to worry about form.

side.boxText: Amit Varma sees the show as one long conversation with threads you can pull: Episodes 25 and 26 and the public choice episode on the state, the episodes on firms, *The Beauty of Finance*, and the episode on education. {#state}

contQuote.text: Build that body of work. It is a repository. And in a sense, it is flow becoming stock. Build that body of work, play the long game.

p3.deck: Four tales from the farewell, and what each one says about making things

stories.caption: never missing a Friday
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the deadline he never missed
stories.head: Twelve o’clock, come what may
body: Amit Varma describes himself as “really bloody minded” about seeing things through once they start. *The Seen and the Unseen* ran weekly for seven years and is now fortnightly, and he has never missed a scheduled release. {#sevenyears}

*Everything is Everything* kept the same discipline: every Friday at 12 o’clock, an episode came out. Once, very early on, it slipped to a Saturday. Otherwise it held, “even when I was in hospital getting a procedure done or Ajay broke his leg”. {128-S02}
The shooting, Varma said, was not a big deal. Once every six weeks the hosts gathered at a friend’s farmhouse and, over three days, shot six episodes, two a day. {#farmhouse}

The burden lay elsewhere. Varma also produced the show. When the editor, Nomsita MS Haritashya, sent him a rough cut, he drew up the painstakingly detailed list of inserts that appear on screen. Then the two of them talked over the edit every day until the episode went out on Friday. Rinse and repeat, every week.
He could bank episodes of *The Seen and the Unseen*, which now comes out fortnightly. Not this one. “This was just on my mind all the time,” he said.
He did not want to stop. “Ajay and I both love the show,” he said. Only when the two talked and found they both had reasons did they agree to let it go.
~ Now, he said, it is time to take a pause, do some writing and “get some chill back in my life”. {#chill}
stories.why: A fixed cadence is a promise to the audience, and this one was kept for two and a half years. The cost, Varma found, was not the shooting but the space it took in his head.

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on how this show escaped the ideas folder
stories.head: Fifty ideas in a folder
body: Amit Varma first tried to persuade Ajay Shah to do a show together three or four years ago, at a conference in Udaipur. He forgets exactly when. {128-S03}
He has discussed many ideas with many people. In a creative-ideas folder in Roam Research, he keeps some fifty YouTube ideas: a solo vlog, a show with this person or that. {#fifty} Most never happen.
What made this one different was that they simply began. “We knew we would be imperfect at the start,” Varma said. “We knew that it would probably be shit.” Some early moments still make them cringe.
~ They started anyway, set the Friday cadence and stuck to it. Only through iteration, Varma said, do you get better.

quote.text: But the difference is that you and I took action. We went into it, we said, let’s just start.

stories.start: A story I keep going back to is I had once recorded an episode
stories.end: But today it's an intimate medium and that's beautiful.
stories.caption: the viewer who interrupted
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the intimacy of a new medium
stories.head: The viewer who butted in
body: Amit Varma once recorded an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* with Abhinandan Sekhri. It is a story, he said, that he keeps going back to. {128-S04}
Someone who watched it later told Varma how it had felt: “I felt so much that I’m sitting with two friends and chatting in my living room that at one point I interrupted you.”
Varma loves the story for what it says about the medium. There was a time when stars were larger than life, he said. Today it is an intimate medium, “and that’s beautiful”.
~ That intimacy, he argued, is why being yourself works. It is easy, it is what people relate to, and it is the only unique thing about you. {#beyourself}
stories.why: In an intimate medium the audience feels like a guest in the room, so a performance shows. Being yourself is the only thing that sets you apart from eight billion others. {#billion}

stories.start: A dear friend of mine who went on to start a successful podcast
stories.end: It is a repository. And in a sense, it is flow becoming stock.
stories.caption: advice to a friend
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s advice to a friend starting a podcast
stories.head: Plan for the binge, not the debut
body: A few years ago, when *The Seen and the Unseen* was doing well, a dear friend of Amit Varma’s asked his advice. She was about to start a podcast of her own. {128-S06}

His advice was not to worry about how her audience would take the first episode. “Don’t think of what your audience will consume on episode one,” he told her. “Think of what they will binge at episode hundred.”
Her podcast, he said, went on to succeed.
~ Worrying about lighting, or about what your friends will say, gets in the way, Varma said. A show is a body of work: each weekly episode is flow, but together they become a repository. {128-C11}
stories.why: Judge a show by the catalogue a new listener can binge, not by the reception of its first week. Weekly flow, kept up long enough, becomes lasting stock, which is how Varma sees this show’s archive.
